description.narrative: Alternatives Espace Citoyens, AEC Over the past thirty (30) years, the situation of women and children in international and non-international armed conflicts has become a matter of global concern, underlining a remarkable evolution in the international community's awareness of the scale and gravity of the suffering inflicted on women and children during armed conflicts. This issue has been the subject of several resolutions adopted by the United Nations General Assembly, one of the earliest being the “Declaration on the Protection of Women and Children in Emergency and Armed Conflict”, adopted in December 1974. With this declaration, the UN member states resolved to condemn and prohibit attacks and bombardments, as well as the use of chemical and bacteriological weapons against the civilian population, in particular women and children, who constitute the most vulnerable part of the population. States also resolved to consider as criminal “all forms of repression and cruel and inhuman treatment of womenand children, in particular imprisonment, torture, shootings, mass arrests, collective punishments, destruction of dwellings and displacement by force, committed by belligerents during military operations or in occupied territories”. In the Declaration on the Protection of Women and Children in Emergency and Armed Conflict, States committed themselves to taking all necessary measures “to ensure the prohibition of measures such as persecution, torture, reprisals, degrading treatment and violence, in particular against women and children, as part of the civilianpopulation”, in accordance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the Declaration of the Rights of the Child and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; in accordance with the provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the Declarationof the Rights of the Child and other international instruments. Despite the clarity of this declaration, which is itself based on the rules and principles of international humanitarian law, the situation of women and children in the context of armed conflict has hardly improved since 1974; and this is unfortunately the case in Niger, a Sahelian country facing, like its neighbors (Burkina Faso, Mali, Nigeria and Chad), a major security crisis. The armed conflict underway in this country has had particularly harmful consequences for women and children, whose most basic rights are totally ignored and violated by the belligerents; and this, in total disregard of the Geneva Conventions and other instruments of international humanitarian law and international human rights law, which clearly provide for protection measures for women and children. In Niger, as in other Sahelian countries affected by the rise of violent extremism, it isimportant to emphasize that the question of women's status and rights is today, for many violent extremist groups,a major ideological issue in the confrontation between the West and Islam; and many observers are unanimous in stressing that the rise of fundamentalism and violent extremism generally leads to a deterioration in the social and political climate, marked in particular by the impossibility of calmly debating issues relating to women's rights. The rise of violent extremism also hampers the activities of women's rights defenders, at a time when violence against women is on the increase and their economic and political status and position are becoming even more fragile.However, despite being recognized as the main victims of the ongoing conflict in the country, women and girls remain largely uninvolved in the various initiatives aimed at promoting and defending their rights in a context where these are particularly at stake; and although it is unanimously recognized that they can play a crucial role in conflict prevention and management, there are few initiatives aimed at valorizing their potential as actors in defending their rights and building peace within their communities. The importance of women's role in conflict prevention and resolution, and in peace-building, wasunderscored by UN Security Council Resolution 1325. This resolution calls for “greater participation by women in decisions taken with a view to the prevention and settlement of disputes”. Aware of the importance of protectingwomen's rights, and with a view to putting UN Security Council Resolutions 1325 and 1820 into practice, the Alternative Espaces Citoyens association has set up a women's rights organization, the Alternative Espaces Citoyens association and the Alliance des femmes pour la paix et la sécurité (APAISE) have decided to initiate the present action with a view to promoting the role and participation of women in conflict prevention and management, as well as setting up a citizen watch mechanism and conducting advocacy and lobbying actions. A. Objectives and resultsThe overall objective of the action is to contribute to the advent and preservation of peace and security in Niger, through initiatives and actions involving women's organizations at national and local level. This overall objective is underpinned by three strategic goals:-Objective 1: By the end of 2025, strengthen the role and participation of women in national and regional conflict prevention and management mechanisms;-Objective 2: Advocate for theadoption, by the end of 2025, of security management policies based on respect for human rights, dialogue, community participation and development initiatives.Through this action, Alternative Espaces Citoyens(AEC) and Alliance pour la paix et la sécurité (APAISE) intend to achieve the following results:-Result 1: By the end of 2025, some120 Nigerien women and girls, the majority from the regions of Agadez, Diffa, Maradi, Tahoua and Tillabery, have acquired skills and abilities in human rights and conflict prevention and management, including early warning, mediation and advocacy; -Result 2: By the end of 2025, respect for human rights, in particular women's rights, dialogue, community participation, including that of women, and development actions areaccepted by public authorities as key elements in the management of security problems.
